questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The manager was angry __________ the employees for their carelessness.
questions.explanation: 'Angry with' is correct when directed at a person. 'On' is wrong — 'angry on' is non-standard. 'At' is wrong — 'angry at' is used more for situations than people in formal English. 'Upon' is wrong — doesn't collocate with 'angry'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about articles:

(i) 'A' is always used before words starting with the letter 'u'.
(ii) 'An' is used before words beginning with a vowel sound, regardless of spelling.
(iii) 'The' is used when the noun is specific or previously mentioned.
(iv) No article is used before abstract nouns in a general sense (e.g., 'Kindness is a virtue').

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'An' before vowel sounds regardless of spelling (i correct — e.g., 'an hour'). 'The' for specific/previously mentioned nouns (ii correct). No article before general abstract nouns (iii correct). (i) is wrong because some 'u' words begin with a vowel sound ('an umbrella') while others have consonant sound ('a university'). '(ii), (iii), (iv) and (i)' includes (i). '(ii) and (iii) only' excludes (iv). '(iii), (iv) and (i) only' includes (i).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The sentence 'I have been living here since five years' is grammatically incorrect.
Reason (R): 'Since' is used with a point of time (since 2019, since Monday), while 'for' is used with a period/duration of time (for five years, for two hours).

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'Since five years' is wrong; it should be 'for five years' (A correct). R explains the since/for distinction — since=point, for=duration (R correct and directly explains the error). 'Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)' is wrong because R explains the exact rule violated. '(A) is correct but (R) is not correct' is wrong because R is correct. '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct' is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following idioms with their meanings:

Column I:
(a) To have an axe to grind
(b) To put all eggs in one basket
(c) To throw cold water on
(d) To blow one's own trumpet

Column II:
(i) To discourage
(ii) To boast about oneself
(iii) To have a selfish motive
(iv) To risk everything on a single venture

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Axe to grind' = selfish motive (iii). 'All eggs in one basket' = risk everything on one venture (iv). 'Throw cold water' = discourage (i). 'Blow own trumpet' = boast (ii). '(a)-(iv), (b)-(iii), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i)' swaps (a) and (b). '(a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii)' swaps (b) and (c). '(a)-(i), (b)-(iv), (c)-(iii), (d)-(ii)' swaps (a) and (c).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences correctly use the present perfect tense?

(i) She has completed her assignment already.
(ii) They have went to the market.
(iii) I have known him since childhood.
(iv) He has wrote three books so far.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Has completed' uses correct past participle (i correct). 'Have known since childhood' is correct present perfect (iii correct). (ii) is wrong — 'went' should be 'gone' (past participle). (iv) is wrong — 'wrote' should be 'written' (past participle). '(i), (ii) and (iii)' includes (ii). '(i), (iii) and (iv)' includes (iv). '(ii) and (iv) only' includes wrong sentences.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct synonym of 'IMPECCABLE':
questions.explanation: 'Impeccable' means without any faults or errors — perfect. 'Flawless' is the correct synonym. 'Faulty' is wrong — it's an antonym. 'Mediocre' is wrong — means average quality. 'Ordinary' is wrong — means commonplace.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The students were prohibited __________ using mobile phones during exams.
questions.explanation: 'Prohibited from' is the correct collocation meaning forbidden. 'To' is wrong — we say 'forbidden to' but 'prohibited from'. 'For' is wrong — doesn't collocate here. 'Against' is wrong — doesn't pair with 'prohibited'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about clauses:

(i) A noun clause functions as subject, object, or complement in a sentence.
(ii) An adjective clause modifies a noun or pronoun and usually begins with who, which, that.
(iii) A main clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.
(iv) An adverb clause modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb and begins with subordinating conjunctions.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Noun clauses function as S/O/C (i correct). Adjective clauses modify nouns with who/which/that (ii correct). Adverb clauses use subordinating conjunctions (iii correct). (iii) is wrong because a main (independent) clause CAN stand alone as a complete sentence — that's its defining feature. '(i), (ii), (iv) and (iii)' includes (iii). '(i) and (ii) only' excludes (iv). '(ii), (iv) and (iii) only' includes (iii).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The sentence 'Neither Ram nor his friends was present' is incorrect.
Reason (R): With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it; since 'friends' (plural) is nearest, the verb should be 'were', not 'was'.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'Was' should be 'were' because 'friends' is nearest (A correct). R states the proximity rule for neither...nor (R correct and explains why 'were' is needed). 'Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)' is wrong because R explains the exact grammar rule. '(A) is correct but (R) is not correct' is wrong because R is correct. '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct' is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following words with their correct antonyms:

Column I:
(a) Prolific
(b) Obsolete
(c) Gregarious
(d) Volatile

Column II:
(i) Stable
(ii) Unproductive
(iii) Modern
(iv) Reclusive

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Prolific (highly productive) ↔ Unproductive (ii). Obsolete (outdated) ↔ Modern (iii). Gregarious (sociable) ↔ Reclusive (solitary) (iv). Volatile (unstable) ↔ Stable (i). '(a)-(iii), (b)-(ii), (c)-(i), (d)-(iv)' swaps (a) and (b). '(a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(iii), (d)-(i)' swaps (b) and (c). '(a)-(i), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii)' swaps (a) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct sentence with proper punctuation:
questions.explanation: Comma after 'said', quotation marks around the speech, period inside the closing quote. 'The teacher said 'Practice makes perfect'.' is wrong — missing comma after 'said'. 'The teacher said, 'Practice makes perfect'' is wrong — missing period at end. 'The teacher, said 'Practice makes perfect.'' is wrong — misplaced comma after 'teacher'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct analogy: Eye : See :: Ear : __________
questions.explanation: An eye is used to see; an ear is used to hear. The analogy is organ:function. 'Sound' is wrong — that's what is heard, not the function of the ear. 'Music' is wrong — too specific. 'Loud' is wrong — that's a quality of sound.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about homophones:

(i) 'Cite' (to quote) and 'Site' (location) and 'Sight' (vision) are homophones.
(ii) 'Waste' (garbage) and 'Waist' (body part) are homophones.
(iii) 'Flour' (powder) and 'Flower' (bloom) are homophones.
(iv) 'Affect' (influence) and 'Effect' (result) are homophones.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Cite/Site/Sight all sound /saɪt/ (i correct). Waste/Waist both sound /weɪst/ (ii correct). Flour/Flower both sound /flaʊər/ (iv correct). (iv) is wrong because 'Affect' (/əˈfɛkt/) and 'Effect' (/ɪˈfɛkt/) have slightly different first vowel sounds — they're commonly confused but NOT true homophones. '(i), (ii), (iv) and (iii)' includes (iv). '(i) and (iii) only' excludes (ii). '(ii), (iv) and (iii) only' includes (iv).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The book is divided __________ twelve chapters.
questions.explanation: 'Divided into' is the correct collocation meaning split/separated into parts. 'In' is wrong — 'divided in' is non-standard. 'To' is wrong — doesn't collocate. 'By' is wrong — 'divided by' is used in mathematics, not for sections.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The words 'compliment' and 'complement' have entirely different meanings.
Reason (R): 'Compliment' means praise or flattery, while 'complement' means something that completes or enhances.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: These words have different meanings (A correct). R defines both correctly — compliment=praise, complement=completes (R correct and demonstrates A). 'Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)' is wrong because R proves A. '(A) is correct but (R) is not correct' is wrong because R is correct. '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct' is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct antonym of 'LOQUACIOUS':
questions.explanation: 'Loquacious' means very talkative. 'Taciturn' (reserved, saying little) is the antonym. 'Talkative' is wrong — it's a synonym. 'Verbose' is wrong — means wordy (synonym direction). 'Garrulous' is wrong — means excessively talkative (synonym).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences uses the correct form of the pronoun?

(i) It is she who deserves the award.
(ii) Between you and I, the plan is flawed.
(iii) Whom do you think will win the election?
(iv) The teacher asked him and me to stay back.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'It is she' — nominative after 'be' (i correct). 'Him and me' — objective as objects of 'asked' (iv correct). (ii) is wrong — should be 'Between you and me' (objective after preposition). (iii) is wrong — should be 'Who do you think will win' ('who' is subject of 'will win'). '(i), (ii) and (iv)' includes (ii). '(i), (iii) and (iv)' includes (iii). '(ii) and (iii) only' includes wrong sentences.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following prepositions with their correct usage:

Column I:
(a) Differ ___
(b) Comply ___
(c) Dispose ___
(d) Preside ___

Column II:
(i) over
(ii) from
(iii) of
(iv) with

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Differ FROM (ii). Comply WITH (iv). Dispose OF (iii). Preside OVER (i). '(a)-(iv), (b)-(ii), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii)' assigns 'differ' to 'with'. '(a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(i)' assigns 'comply' to 'of'. '(a)-(i), (b)-(iv), (c)-(iii), (d)-(ii)' assigns 'differ' to 'over'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The company has been __________ (grow) steadily since its inception in 2010.
questions.explanation: 'Has been growing' is Present Perfect Continuous (has been + V-ing) for an ongoing action from the past. 'Grown' is wrong — 'has been grown' would be passive, not appropriate here. 'Grew' is wrong — simple past, doesn't work with 'has been'. 'Grow' is wrong — base form doesn't follow 'has been'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the correct meaning of the idiom 'To eat humble pie':
options: To apologize and admit one's error
To be forced to eat leftovers
questions.correctAnswer: To apologize and admit one's error
questions.explanation: 'Eat humble pie' means to accept humiliation by admitting a mistake. 'Enjoy a simple meal' is wrong — literal misreading. 'Suffer from poverty' is wrong — unrelated meaning. 'Eat leftovers' is wrong — literal misinterpretation.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct sentence:
options: The committee have decided to postpone the meeting.
The committee has decided to postpone the meeting.
The committee has decided to postponed the meeting.
The committee have decided to postponing the meeting.
questions.correctAnswer: The committee has decided to postpone the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Committee' as a collective noun takes singular verb 'has'. 'To postpone' (infinitive) follows 'decided'. 'The committee have decided to postpone the meeting.' is wrong — 'have' doesn't agree with singular collective. 'The committee has decided to postponed the meeting.' is wrong — 'to postponed' is grammatically wrong (infinitive needs base form). 'The committee have decided to postponing the meeting.' is wrong — both 'have' and 'to postponing' are wrong.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about tenses:

(i) Future Perfect: 'will have + past participle' — for actions completed by a future time.
(ii) Past Continuous: 'was/were + past participle' — for ongoing past actions.
(iii) Past Perfect Continuous: 'had been + V-ing' — for ongoing actions before a past event.
(iv) Simple Present: used for habitual actions and universal truths.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Future Perfect = will have + V3 (i correct). Past Perfect Continuous = had been + V-ing (ii correct). Simple Present for habits/truths (iii correct). (ii) is wrong because Past Continuous uses 'was/were + present participle (-ing)', NOT past participle. 'Was written' is passive, not continuous. '(i), (iii), (iv) and (ii)' includes (ii). '(i) and (iv) only' excludes (iii). '(iii), (iv) and (ii) only' includes (ii).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 'Who' and 'whom' cannot be used interchangeably.
Reason (R): 'Who' is a subjective pronoun (used as subject) while 'whom' is an objective pronoun (used as object of a verb or preposition).

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Who/whom are not interchangeable (A correct). Who=subject, whom=object (R correct and explains the grammatical distinction). 'Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)' is wrong because R explains the rule directly. '(A) is correct but (R) is not correct' is wrong because R is correct. '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct' is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct synonym of 'DAUNTLESS':
questions.explanation: 'Dauntless' means showing no fear — brave/courageous. 'Fearless' is the synonym. 'Timid' is wrong — antonym (fearful). 'Cautious' is wrong — means careful/wary. 'Hesitant' is wrong — means uncertain/reluctant.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following analogies:

Column I:
(a) Cobbler : Shoes
(b) Carpenter : Furniture
(c) Tailor : Clothes
(d) Mason : Walls

Column II:
(i) Builds/constructs with bricks
(ii) Repairs and makes footwear
(iii) Makes and repairs garments
(iv) Makes items from wood

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Cobbler works with shoes (ii). Carpenter works with wood/furniture (iv). Tailor makes clothes (iii). Mason builds with bricks (i). '(a)-(iv), (b)-(ii), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii)' swaps (a) and (b). '(a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(i)' swaps (b) and (c). '(a)-(i), (b)-(iv), (c)-(iii), (d)-(ii)' swaps (a) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: She is devoted __________ her family.
questions.explanation: 'Devoted to' is the correct fixed collocation. 'For' is wrong — doesn't pair with 'devoted'. 'With' is wrong — non-standard. 'Towards' is wrong — while sometimes used, 'to' is standard with 'devoted'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct antonym of 'ZEALOUS':
questions.explanation: 'Zealous' means having great enthusiasm/passion. 'Apathetic' (showing no interest/concern) is the antonym. 'Enthusiastic' is wrong — synonym. 'Passionate' is wrong — synonym. 'Fervent' is wrong — synonym (intensely enthusiastic).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about punctuation:

(i) A semicolon joins two related independent clauses without a conjunction.
(ii) A colon introduces a list, quotation, or explanation.
(iii) An apostrophe in 'it's' always shows possession.
(iv) Commas are used to separate items in a list.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Semicolons join related independent clauses (i correct). Colons introduce lists/explanations (ii correct). Commas separate list items (iv correct). (iii) is wrong because 'it's' = 'it is' (contraction), NOT possession — possessive 'its' has NO apostrophe. '(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)' includes (iii). '(i) and (iv) only' excludes (ii). '(ii), (iii) and (iv) only' includes (iii).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The sentence 'The cattle is grazing in the field' is incorrect.
Reason (R): 'Cattle' is always a plural noun and requires a plural verb — the correct form is 'The cattle are grazing'.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'Cattle is' is wrong; should be 'cattle are' (A correct). 'Cattle' is a plural-only noun requiring plural verb (R correct and explains the error). 'Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)' is wrong because R explains the grammar rule. '(A) is correct but (R) is not correct' is wrong because R is correct. '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct' is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the correct meaning of the idiom 'To be in the doldrums':
options: To be at the top of success
To be in a dangerous situation
To be in a state of depression or inactivity
questions.correctAnswer: To be in a state of depression or inactivity
questions.explanation: 'In the doldrums' means feeling depressed or experiencing a period of stagnation. 'Extremely happy' is wrong — opposite. 'Top of success' is wrong — unrelated. 'Dangerous situation' is wrong — not the meaning.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The child is too young __________ understand such complex concepts.
questions.explanation: 'Too + adjective + to + infinitive' is the correct structure. 'For' is wrong — 'too young for understanding' would need restructuring. 'That' is wrong — doesn't fit this structure. 'So' is wrong — 'so young' needs 'that' after it.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following sentence types with examples:

Column I:
(a) Noun Clause
(b) Adjective Clause
(c) Adverb Clause
(d) Main Clause

Column II:
(i) 'He left because he was tired.'
(ii) 'What he said was surprising.'
(iii) 'She works in a hospital.'
(iv) 'The man who helped us was kind.'

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'What he said' is a noun clause (subject) (ii). 'Who helped us' is an adjective clause modifying 'man' (iv). 'Because he was tired' is an adverb clause of reason (i). 'She works in a hospital' is an independent/main clause (iii). '(a)-(iv), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii), (d)-(i)' swaps (a) and (b). '(a)-(ii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(iii)' swaps (b) and (c). '(a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii)' swaps (a) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct tense: If I __________ (know) about the meeting, I would have attended.
questions.explanation: Third conditional (unreal past): 'If + past perfect, would have + past participle'. 'Had known' is correct. 'Have known' is wrong — that's present perfect. 'Knew' is wrong — that's second conditional (present unreal). 'Was knowing' is wrong — 'know' is stative and doesn't take continuous.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct synonym of 'AMELIORATE':
questions.explanation: 'Ameliorate' means to make something better/improve it. 'Worsen' is wrong — antonym. 'Destroy' is wrong — means to demolish. 'Maintain' is wrong — means to keep the same, not improve.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following pairs of words are correctly identified as homophones?

(i) Pale — Pail
(ii) Hear — Here
(iii) Accept — Except
(iv) Seize — Sees

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: Pale/Pail both sound /peɪl/ (i correct). Hear/Here both sound /hɪər/ (ii correct). (iii) is wrong — Accept /əkˈsɛpt/ and Except /ɪkˈsɛpt/ have different first syllables. (iv) is wrong — Seize /siːz/ and Sees /siːz/ may sound similar but 'seize' has a z-sound while 'sees' has an s-sound at the end in careful speech. '(i), (ii) and (iv)' includes (iv). '(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)' includes (iii) and (iv). '(ii), (iii) and (iv) only' includes (iii) and (iv).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The sentence 'He is more intelligent than me' is considered acceptable in modern English.
Reason (R): While traditionally 'than I' (nominative) is prescribed, modern usage widely accepts 'than me' (objective) in informal contexts.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'More intelligent than me' is accepted in modern usage (A correct). R explains the evolution from prescriptive 'than I' to acceptable 'than me' in contemporary English (R correct and explains A). 'Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)' is wrong because R explains the linguistic basis. '(A) is correct but (R) is not correct' is wrong because R is correct. '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct' is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The students are preparing __________ the examination.
questions.explanation: 'Preparing for' is the correct collocation meaning getting ready for something. 'To' is wrong — 'prepare to' needs an infinitive after. 'Of' is wrong — doesn't collocate. 'With' is wrong — doesn't pair correctly here.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following words with their synonyms:

Column I:
(a) Arduous
(b) Clandestine
(c) Dilapidated
(d) Exorbitant

Column II:
(i) Excessive
(ii) Secret
(iii) Ruined
(iv) Difficult

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Arduous = Difficult (iv). Clandestine = Secret (ii). Dilapidated = Ruined/in disrepair (iii). Exorbitant = Excessive (i). '(a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii)' swaps (a) and (b). '(a)-(iv), (b)-(iii), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i)' swaps (b) and (c). '(a)-(i), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii), (d)-(iv)' swaps (a) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct sentence using passive voice:
options: The bridge was being construct when the accident happened.
The bridge being constructed when the accident happened.
The bridge was being constructed when the accident happened.
The bridge was construct when the accident happened.
questions.correctAnswer: The bridge was being constructed when the accident happened.
questions.explanation: Past Continuous Passive = was/were + being + past participle. 'Was being constructed' is correct. 'The bridge was being construct when the accident happened.' is wrong — 'construct' should be 'constructed'. 'The bridge being constructed when the accident happened.' is wrong — missing 'was'. 'The bridge was construct when the accident happened.' is wrong — missing 'being' and using base form.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about commonly confused words:

(i) 'Elicit' and 'Illicit' have the same meaning.
(ii) 'Principle' means a fundamental rule; 'Principal' means head/chief or main.
(iii) 'Advice' (noun) means suggestion; 'Advise' (verb) means to give suggestion.
(iv) 'Emigrate' means to leave one's country; 'Immigrate' means to enter a new country.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Principle/Principal distinction (i correct). Advice(n)/Advise(v) distinction (ii correct). Emigrate(leave)/Immigrate(enter) (iii correct). (i) is wrong — 'Elicit' means to draw out/extract (a response), while 'Illicit' means illegal/unlawful — completely different meanings. '(ii), (iii), (iv) and (i)' includes (i). '(ii) and (iii) only' excludes (iv). '(iii), (iv) and (i) only' includes (i).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'To see eye to eye':
questions.explanation: 'See eye to eye' means to be in full agreement. 'Stare angrily' is wrong — literal misreading. 'Excellent eyesight' is wrong — unrelated. 'Look closely' is wrong — different meaning.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Collective nouns like 'team', 'committee', 'jury' can take either singular or plural verbs.
Reason (R): When the group acts as a single unit, a singular verb is used; when members act individually, a plural verb is used.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Collective nouns can take singular or plural verbs (A correct). The choice depends on whether the group acts as one or individually (R correct and explains the rule). 'Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)' is wrong because R explains the conditions. '(A) is correct but (R) is not correct' is wrong because R is correct. '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct' is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: He has a __________ (tendency) to procrastinate when faced with difficult tasks.
questions.explanation: 'Tendency' is the correct spelling of the noun meaning an inclination or propensity towards something, as in a tendency to procrastinate. 'Tendancy' is wrong — it misspells the second syllable with an 'a', a very common error influenced by words such as 'attendance'. 'Tendence' is wrong — it is not a current English word; the noun formed from 'tend' in this sense is 'tendency'. 'Tendensy' is wrong — it substitutes an 's' for the 'c' and has no basis in English orthography.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct analogy: Judge : Court :: Pilot : __________
questions.explanation: A judge works in a court; a pilot works in a cockpit. The analogy is profession:workspace. 'Airport' is wrong — too broad, not the specific workspace. 'Airplane' is wrong — that's the vehicle, not the workspace within it. 'Sky' is wrong — too broad.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the use of articles with geographical names:

(i) 'The' is used before plural island groups (the Andamans, the Maldives).
(ii) 'The' is used before all lakes (the Dal Lake, the Wular Lake).
(iii) 'The' is used before deserts (the Sahara, the Thar).
(iv) No article is used before individual islands (Sri Lanka, Madagascar).

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'The' before plural islands (i correct). 'The' before deserts (ii correct). No article before individual islands (iii correct). (ii) is wrong — most lakes do NOT take 'the' (it's 'Dal Lake', not 'the Dal Lake'; 'Lake Superior', not 'the Lake Superior'). '(i), (iii), (iv) and (ii)' includes (ii). '(i) and (iii) only' excludes (iv). '(iii), (iv) and (ii) only' includes (ii).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Had I knew earlier, I would have helped you.
If I had know earlier, I would have helped you.
Had I known earlier, I will have helped you.
Had I known earlier, I would have helped you.
questions.correctAnswer: Had I known earlier, I would have helped you.
questions.explanation: Inverted third conditional: 'Had + subject + past participle, would have + past participle'. 'Had I knew earlier, I would have helped you.' is wrong — 'knew' should be 'known'. 'If I had know earlier, I would have helped you.' is wrong — 'know' should be 'known'. 'Had I known earlier, I will have helped you.' is wrong — 'will have' should be 'would have' (past unreal).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following words with their correct definitions:

Column I:
(a) Eminent
(b) Imminent
(c) Immanent
(d) Emanate

Column II:
(i) About to happen soon
(ii) Existing within; inherent
(iii) Famous and distinguished
(iv) To originate from

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Eminent = famous/distinguished (iii). Imminent = about to happen (i). Immanent = inherent/existing within (ii). Emanate = originate from (iv). '(a)-(i), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii)' swaps (a) and (b). '(a)-(iii), (b)-(ii), (c)-(i), (d)-(iv)' swaps (b) and (c). '(a)-(iv), (b)-(i), (c)-(ii), (d)-(iii)' swaps (a) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct antonym of 'PRISTINE':
questions.explanation: 'Pristine' means in its original condition/unspoiled/pure. 'Contaminated' (polluted/spoiled) is the antonym. 'Pure' is wrong — synonym. 'Clean' is wrong — synonym. 'Fresh' is wrong — similar direction.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct preposition: The police are inquiring __________ the matter thoroughly.
questions.explanation: 'Inquire into' means to investigate formally. 'About' is wrong — 'inquire about' means to ask for information, not investigate. 'On' is wrong — doesn't collocate with 'inquire'. 'For' is wrong — doesn't pair here.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about sentence correction:

(i) 'Each of the students have their own locker' — verb error ('have' should be 'has').
(ii) 'The data shows a clear trend' — 'data' can take singular verb in modern usage.
(iii) 'He is one of those who believes in hard work' — no error.
(iv) 'Less people attended today' — 'less' should be 'fewer' before countable nouns.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'Each' needs singular 'has' (i correct). 'Data shows' accepted in modern English (ii correct). 'Fewer' for countable nouns, not 'less' (iii correct). (iii) is wrong — it should be 'who believe' (plural, because 'those' is the antecedent of 'who', not 'one'). '(i), (ii), (iv) and (iii)' includes (iii). '(i) and (iv) only' excludes (ii). '(ii), (iv) and (iii) only' includes (iii).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The words 'there', 'their', and 'they're' are often confused in writing.
Reason (R): All three words are pronounced identically (/ðɛr/) but have different meanings: 'there' (place), 'their' (possessive), 'they're' (contraction of they are).

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: These three words are commonly confused (A correct). R explains they sound the same but mean different things (R correct and explains why confusion occurs). 'Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)' is wrong because R explains the root cause. '(A) is correct but (R) is not correct' is wrong because R is correct. '(A) is not correct but (R) is correct' is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct idiom to complete: After years of disagreement, the two brothers finally decided to __________.
questions.explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' = make peace after a conflict. 'Break the ice' is wrong — means to start a conversation in an awkward situation. 'Bite the bullet' is wrong — means to endure something painful. 'Beat around the bush' is wrong — means to avoid the main topic.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences contain a dangling modifier?

(i) Walking down the street, the building caught my attention.
(ii) After finishing the exam, the students left the hall.
(iii) Having studied all night, the test was easy for him.
(iv) While eating dinner, she watched the news.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) 'Walking down the street' dangles — buildings don't walk (correct identification of dangling modifier). (iii) 'Having studied all night' dangles — the test didn't study (correct). (ii) is correct — 'students' logically did the finishing. (iv) is correct — 'she' logically did the eating. '(i), (ii) and (iii)' includes (ii). '(i), (iii) and (iv)' includes (iv). '(ii) and (iv) only' includes wrong sentences.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct synonym of 'ADMONISH':
questions.explanation: 'Admonish' means to warn or reprimand firmly. 'Warn' is the closest synonym. 'Praise' is wrong — antonym. 'Encourage' is wrong — opposite direction. 'Reward' is wrong — means to give recognition/prize.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following literary terms with their definitions:

Column I:
(a) Simile
(b) Metaphor
(c) Personification
(d) Hyperbole

Column II:
(i) Extreme exaggeration for effect
(ii) Direct comparison using 'like' or 'as'
(iii) Giving human qualities to non-human things
(iv) Implied comparison without 'like' or 'as'

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Simile uses 'like/as' for comparison (ii). Metaphor is implied comparison (iv). Personification gives human qualities (iii). Hyperbole is exaggeration (i). '(a)-(iv), (b)-(ii), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii)' swaps (a) and (b). '(a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(iv), (d)-(i)' swaps (b) and (c). '(a)-(i), (b)-(iv), (c)-(iii), (d)-(ii)' swaps (a) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The government should take measures to __________ (erode / eradicate) corruption from society.
questions.explanation: 'Eradicate' means to completely remove/destroy something — fits 'corruption'. 'Erode' is wrong — means to gradually wear away (doesn't collocate well with active measures against corruption). 'Erect' is wrong — means to build/construct. 'Erupt' is wrong — means to burst out suddenly.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Scarcely he had reached the station when the train departed.
Scarcely had he reached the station then the train departed.
Scarcely has he reached the station when the train departed.
Scarcely had he reached the station when the train departed.
questions.correctAnswer: Scarcely had he reached the station when the train departed.
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely + had + subject + past participle + when...' is the correct structure with inversion. 'Scarcely he had reached the station when the train departed.' is wrong — no inversion (should be 'had he'). 'Scarcely had he reached the station then the train departed.' is wrong — 'then' should be 'when'. 'Scarcely has he reached the station when the train departed.' is wrong — 'has' should be 'had' for past context.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct analogy: Flock : Birds :: Pack : __________
questions.explanation: A 'flock' is a group of birds; a 'pack' is a group of wolves. 'Cattle' is wrong — group of cattle is a 'herd'. 'Bees' is wrong — group of bees is a 'swarm'. 'Fish' is wrong — group of fish is a 'shoal' or 'school'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about voice change (active/passive):

(i) 'By' is always required in passive voice.
(ii) Only transitive verbs (with objects) can be changed to passive voice.
(iii) In passive voice, the object of active voice becomes the subject.
(iv) Passive voice uses 'be + past participle'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Only transitive verbs can be passivized (i correct). Object becomes subject (ii correct). Passive uses be + V3 (iv correct). (i) is wrong because 'by + agent' can be omitted when the agent is unknown or unimportant (e.g., 'The window was broken' — no 'by' needed). '(ii), (iii), (i) and (iv)' includes (i). '(ii) and (iv) only' excludes (iii). '(iii), (i) and (iv) only' includes (i).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct antonym of 'PERNICIOUS':
questions.explanation: 'Pernicious' means having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual way. 'Beneficial' (advantageous/helpful) is the antonym. 'Harmful' is wrong — synonym. 'Destructive' is wrong — synonym. 'Lethal' is wrong — synonym (deadly).
